4FOREWORD
As part of its effort to strengthen the UN system’s capacity to fulfil its development mandate, the UN 
Secretary General introduced the United Nations Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) in 1997. 
This new program development tool is intended to be a planning framework that lays the foundation for the 
co-operation of UN Programmes, Funds and Agencies in a given country. It is a means to achieve the “goal 
oriented collaboration, coherence and mutual reinforcement” called for by General Assembly Resolution 
53/192. 
The UN team joint program development effort commenced when the UN Resident Co-ordinator in Egypt 
called upon all UN Agencies to actively participate in the preparation of the Common Country Assessment 
(CCA) for Egypt. All UN Agencies represented in Cairo as well as the World Bank joined forces to 
produce the first CCA in 2001. United Nations Agencies and Programmes were organised in thematic 
groups which worked closely with Government of Egypt counterparts on specific subjects. 
Following presentation of the CCA to the Egyptian Government in May 2001, the UN Team in Egypt set 
out to prepare the UNDAF. In the meantime, the majority of UN Specialised Agencies, Funds and 
Programmes commenced preparation of their own country programmes of assistance for the medium term. 
A review of individual assistance programmes revealed that the findings of the CCA exercise had been 
fully taken into account by both the UN and the Government in preparing Agency or Programme country 
plans. 
The present common framework is the result of an intensive process of consultations. Successive drafts 
have been discussed by the UN Agencies with their respective Government counterparts and finally 
presented by the UN country team to the Ministry of State for Foreign Affairs – International Cooperation. 
In addition, discussions took place both with representatives of the civil society and of the donor 
community, through the DAG - Donors Assistance Group. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt
6I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
1.Purpose of UNDAF
UNDAF is a planning framework that lays the foundation for UN system cooperation with Egypt during the 
period 2002-2006 and provides an overall guidance for UN Agencies and Funds to develop their own 
programs of development assistance in a mutually reinforcing and goal oriented manner. The UNDAF 
process began with the preparation of the Common Country Assessment (CCA) in 2001. All UN Agencies 
represented in Egypt (including the World Bank), as well as government counterparts participated in 
preparing this common diagnosis of the country’s development on which the UNDAF is based. 
2. UN role in Egypt
Egypt played a central role in world history long before anyone recorded historical events and the Arab 
Republic of Egypt, as it is known today, still deeply influences international affairs. What the Egyptian 
government does has immediate repercussions in other Arab states and affects world relations. Egypt is, 
consequently, a key country for the United Nations. 
Egypt’s economic development strategy has been successful in quantitative terms. Impressive results have 
been obtained in achieving economic stability, reducing fiscal deficit and inflation and liberalizing the 
economy. Key social indicators, such as immunization coverage, mortality rates and life expectancy at birth 
have also shown remarkable improvements and continue on a sustained positive trend. On the other hand, 
the benefits of growth have not been equally distributed. Low-income groups in general and large 
proportions of women, youth and rural dwellers of Upper Egypt, in particular, cannot satisfy their basic 
needs. 
The CCA diagnosis concludes that Egypt has the capacity and the resources to improve its economic and 
social performance and its overall Human Development Index. A modest HDI of 0.642 ranks Egypt 115 in 
the world wide classification and this is hardly compatible with its potential and international standing. To 
achieve equitable and well balanced growth and to integrate vulnerable population groups into the 
economy, Egypt must make better and fuller use of its own national resources as well as of its international 
development assistance programs. The overarching goal for UN system development cooperation has 
therefore been identified as: promoting a more people centered development strategy based on rational and 
efficient use of Egypt’s institutional capabilities, natural resources and human assets. 
3. Rationale for UN system assistance
The UN Agencies, Programmes and Funds (including the World Bank) will continue to help building the 
country’s capacity to deal with its development challenges in their particular fields of concern. UN 
sponsored programs are already affecting, directly or indirectly, the lives of millions of Egyptians and these 
efforts will be pursued and consolidated in the light of lessons learned from past development assistance. 
The UNDAF process has revealed the following: 
• The UN is most successful when it supports government in areas where it has comparative advantages, 
has established a best practice and where it manages to engage the government in a sustained policy 
dialogue. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt
8
• Most benefits accrue when the UN is capable of assisting the government in establishing and 
maintaining close partnerships with other stakeholders and improved coordination practices. 
• Increased involvement of civil society is necessary to promote Egypt´s economic and social 
development and improve delivery of services particularly at the local level in impoverished 
communities. 
• Reducing disparities in Egypt requires a more geographically focussed and systematic approach in 
planning, targeting, implementing and monitoring of development activities. 
• Scattered and uncoordinated UN supported development projects have sometimes not resulted in 
sustainable development. 
Such lessons have been fully taken into account for rationalizing future UN assistance to Egypt. 
Consequently, in promoting a people centered development based on a more rational use of Egypt own 
resources the UN System, through UNDAF, will attempt to make fuller use of its collective comparative 
advantages, such as: 
• Recognized responsibility for leading the world community towards the attainment of the millennium 
targets. 
• Unique role as an interlocutor of the government of Egypt, the donor community and Egyptian civil 
society. 
• Capacity to engage in a policy level dialogue on critical and crosscutting issues for Egypt’s 
development. 
• Collective field practical experience in combating poverty and promoting human development. 
4. Goals and objectives of UN development cooperation 
UNDAF has identified three goals that will assist in maximizing Egypt’s institutional capabilities, natural 
resources and human assets, and the effectiveness of UN development cooperation as a whole. Such goals 
are: 
GOAL I. Enhanced governance through a more participatory dialogue, institutional 
capacity building and civil society empowerment. 
Under this goal, UNDAF has identified 7 development objectives. The UN will firstly assist all 
stakeholders in Egypt’s development to establish a common body of knowledge (facts, figures, trends, etc.), 
on Egypt’s social and economic reality and a common understanding of the nature of development 
problems and constraints. This is a fundamental basis for deepening and widening a dialogue leading to 
well-founded recommendations for economic and social policy formulation and for legal and regulatory 
framework adjustments. Under objective 2 the UN will, as a matter of priority, promote a dialogue on 
issues related to the attainment of the Millenium Development Goals (MDG’s) consistently with 
Government priorities. Policy dialogue will also be concerned with the country’s institutional preparedness 
for the challenges of the future. 
Under objective 3 the UN System will support structural reforms in civil service, public enterprises, 
financial and banking sector, decentralization, investment and export strategies while promoting civil 
society empowerment, local governance and equity concerns. The fourth objective deals with job creation 
and advising on employment policies, particularly for women and youth, to accompany economic growth. 
SME’s business incubators and training centers will be supported as an integral part of this strategy. The 
complex challenges facing the health and education sectors in Egypt will also be tackled (objectives 5 and 6) under this overall goal. An innovative approach to develop the Information and Communication 
Technology sector will also be attempted under objective 7. 
GOAL II. Enhanced natural resources management, environmental sustainability and 
food security. 
The UN System will promote a common understanding of environmental problems and an open dialogue 
facilitating the involvement of civil society and NGOs, improving coordination, sharing best practices and 
methodologies, institutional capacity building, information and training activities, and policy advice as 
required. 
UN objectives under this goal will be concerned with three key issues. In the first place (objective 8), to 
assist Egypt to comply with international environmental law standards on the treatment of solid and liquid 
wastes, hazardous industrial and hospital effluents, harmful gas emissions and the consolidation of 
techniques to preserve fragile ecosystems such as desert borders, oasis and coral reefs. Egyptian 
environmental laws are appropriate but compliance is faulty as a result of general environmental hazard 
unawareness which leads to an uncooperative public attitude. 
Under objective 9 the UN will help the government to critically review food security policies and strategies 
for this largely food deficient country. This touches on a wide variety of problems from re-focussing the 
food subsidy program to a better understanding of the diversity of issues affecting the household food 
economy in Egyptian society. All this will, in turn, need to be reviewed in the light of the very successful 
agricultural reforms of the eighties and the new possibilities offered by Egypt’s accession to the WTO and 
its partnership agreement with the European Union. Finally (objective 10), a set of UN programs and 
projects will be exclusively concerned with maximizing water use efficiency. 
GOAL III. Poverty reduction with emphasis on addressing social and geographical 
disparities. 
In addition to its work at the policy level the UN System in Egypt will, within the limits of its own 
resources, continue addressing directly the needs of the underprivileged sectors of society. UN Agencies 
have been dealing with poverty problems in their particular sector of concern and in accordance with their 
traditional mandates and will continue to do so through their individual programs of assistance. The 
UNDAF however has identified three critical areas which require particular attention and deserve to be 
addressed with renewed commitment and effectiveness. These are: women; children and youth and the 
impoverished rural communities of Upper Egypt. Lessons learned from experiences worldwide indicate 
that in order to make more effective progress in these areas a more systematic and coherent approach is 
necessary from all stakeholders including, first and foremost, the beneficiaries themselves. 
In the case of programs directed at target groups (women, children and youth) the UNDAF acknowledges 
the impressive progress that has taken place nationwide in the last decades in combating disease, preventing 
early death, increasing health standards and ensuring access to education. Such progress and benefits have, 
however, been unevenly distributed. Overcoming disparities that still persist will require a more coherent 
approach from all concerned to Egyptian society’s underprivileged groups. UNDAF aims at facilitating the 
very difficult task of getting actors to achieve a greater collective impact. It will first be necessary to get a 
more realistic and dissagregated statistical information, identify areas of urgent need and set realistic targets 
to be met by year 2006 in line with the Millennium Development Goals. Specialized national policy 
working groups under government leadership involving valid national and international interlocutors will UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

need to be either put in place, or strengthened when they already exist. A careful joint review and 
monitoring mechanism on progress should be set up to feedback and enrich policy decisions, consistently 
with what is being proposed under Goals I and II. 
In the case of territorial targets the UN will aim at combating poverty at the local level by fostering an 
enabling environment for the promotion of participatory local development, provision of basic services, 
generation of family income and strengthening local governance to ensure economic, political and 
environmental sustainability. The specific approach to be adopted in each community may vary according 
to the local context. However it should contain some strategic elements that are essential to engage the 
support of the local population, strengthen local institutions and ensure the sustainability of human 
development achievements. Above all, lessons learned from successful experiences and best practices 
should be subject to critical review by a high-level participatory national policy working group on poverty 
reduction. 
5. Cooperation strategies
In making use of its resources, the UN Specialized Agencies and Programmes in Egypt must privilege the 
unique qualitative value of their contribution as individual entities and as a collective force. The UN can 
help both the government, Egyptian civil society and the international community to tackle and eventually 
resolve some long standing problems that remain an obstacle to Egypt’s human development performance. 
The UNDAF strategy stems from the conclusion of the Common Country Assessment that “Egypt has the 
knowledge and capacity to address the development challenges it faces. Putting the knowledge together in 
appropriate forms for policy makers, donors and the public and making certain that it is effectively shared 
for action is where the challenge lies”. The CCA concludes that the human, technical, institutional and 
financial resources to deal with broad development problems are generally available but poorly organized 
and coordinated so the end result falls below expectations. An effort is needed to pool these resources and 
organize activities in a more systemic manner so that people, technicians, the business community, NGOs, 
public institutions, funding agencies and national economic and political decision makers can act in greater 
harmony towards shared goals. A primary concern that will guide UNDAF throughout this period will be to 
what extent this effort succeeds in helping Egypt meet its contribution to the attainment of the Millenium 
Development Goals. 
Some of the areas identified as goals of the UNDAF will require the adoption of policies, laws and 
regulations by the executive and legislative powers of Egypt. They will also require a commitment to 
change by decision makers, executive officers, politicians, opinion leaders and the Egyptian society as a 
whole. The UN will work to enlist the support of government and society leaders who can act as agents of 
change and produce a multiplier effect on the community at large. To do this, the UN must state its case 
clearly and present a solid front with a common opinion and a single voice. The UN will also promote, in 
agreement with the government, the holding of public for to openly discuss, where applicable, the need for 
change. A major component of UN advocacy work has to do with public information and reaching the 
population at large. Publicity and awareness campaigns to bring about attitudinal readiness for the 
challenges of a changing world or for modifying attitudes and traditions that are discriminatory against 
particular human groups or individuals will also be strategically supported as part of the UN advocacy role
under UNDAF. 
One of the key strategies for the UN system is to promote a more fluid policy dialogue in practically all the 
issues which have been identified as constraints on Egypt’s development. The size of the country, the magnitude and complexity of the issues involved, and their crosscutting nature, has in many cases rendered 
a frank participatory policy dialogue very difficult. The UN system in Egypt is convinced of the necessity 
to promote this exchange of views among all stakeholders on the development objectives identified under 
the UNDAF. This upgraded policy dialogue with the government, and other national and international 
partners in development, constitutes one of the pillars of the UNDAF strategy. 
The UNDAF strategy will fully utilize existing coordinating mechanisms with the government, the donor 
community and civil society to address key development problems holistically and in ways that can 
produce measurable and verifiable impact in the medium term. A relevant co-ordination mechanism is the 
DAG–Donors Assistance Group, an informal network of donor countries that aims to improve the 
effectiveness of development assistance programs. The Resident Coordinator will act as chairman to the 
Donor Assistance Group over the next two years. This Group is operating smoothly in Egypt and in good 
harmony with the Egyptian government counterparts which have fully appreciated the value of a donor coordination mechanism. The DAG should further facilitate and support government leadership in donors’ 
coordination 
Another important element of the UNDAF strategy will be to achieve a better alignment of UN technical 
assistance programs. Further to the CCA exercise, UN Agencies and Programmes have been streamlined in 
at least two ways. First, the timing and duration of Agency programs has been set to coincide with the 
UNDAF time frame which means that henceforth the programming cycles of UN Agencies in Egypt will 
coincide. This is a valuable step forward because program schedule incompatibilities has been a major 
obstacle to get UN Agencies together at a time when decisions are taken. Secondly, the programs 
themselves are based on the findings of the CCA and have been harmonized with UNDAF. This ensures a 
common perspective on the problems to be tackled and consequently opens the way for improved UN 
system co-ordination and program complementarities in the future. 
An innovative feature of the UNDAF for Egypt is that it will attempt to demonstrate that the 
abovementioned strategies that involve UN advocacy work, upgraded policy dialogue, improved donor 
coordination and civil society involvement will be instrumental in assisting the government to increase the 
effectiveness of its poverty eradication programs. Through UNDAF, it is expected that poverty affecting 
vulnerable target groups, namely women and children, and upper Egypt rural areas will be subject to a 
much more coherent and systematic reduction strategy. By concentrating and intensifying its fight against 
poverty in these target groups and neglected areas Egypt will considerably improve its national HDI and 
greatly increase its possibilities to meet MDGs commitments. 
The formulation of the UNDAF has been accompanied by the preparation of the baseline analysis on 
Egypt’s progress towards the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals. Throughout the UNDAF 
cycle successive MDGs reports will be produced with a view to keep track of country progress in 
implementing the international development agenda that resulted from the UN global conferences and their 
follow up meetings. 
In addition, the UN system will build on recent successful experience on joint programming and, whenever 
possible, undertake joint development initiatives that will reinforce an innovative dimension of the Country 
Team’s cooperation with Egypt. 
The Resident Coordinator will ensure appropriate follow up on the implementation of the UNDAF, 
including through a mid-term review in 2004. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt
12
II. RATIONALE
1. Background Information
Egypt played a central role in world history long before anyone recorded historical events. For centuries it 
was one of the world’s centres deeply influencing classical philosophers, and today Egyptian civilisation is 
universally acknowledged as one of the pillars of mankind’s cultural heritage. 
 
The Arab Republic of Egypt, as it is known today, covers approximately one million square kilometres. It 
has a population of over 65 million- the largest in the Arab world- and a GNP of over U$ 85.000 million. 
Its GDP per capita of U$ 1529 has now placed Egypt in the lower middle income countries. The Arab 
Republic of Egypt has played a prominent role in international affairs. During the cold war Egyptian 
diplomacy was actively engaged in East-West relations and simultaneously as a mediator and peace seeker 
in the Arab Israeli conflict. Egypt’s cautious external relation policies have been a reference for all. The 
events of 11 September 2001 will most probably call on Egypt once again to provide guidance to world 
leaders in promoting dialogue, tolerance and mutual respect between nations and peoples of all creeds in 
years to come. 
In short, Egypt is a large and important country by any standards. Furthermore, what Egypt does has 
immediate repercussions in other Arab states and affects world relations. Egypt is, consequently, a key 
country for the United Nations. 
Egypt’s economic development strategy in the last decade has involved cautious and gradual reforms and 
has been undeniably successful in quantitative terms. The Economic Reform and Structural Adjustment 
Programme (ERSAP) initiated in 1990-91, based on market liberalisation and privatisation has restored 
macro economic stability, drastically reduced inflation and fiscal deficit and improved the environment for 
private sector economic activity. GDP growth rate went from an average of 3.5 % in 1990/5 to 5 % in 1996 
and 6,4 % in 2000. Rising purchasing power in Egypt’s large domestic market has fuelled the economy. 
Tourism, the Suez Canal revenues and remittances from Egyptian nationals abroad, provide around U$ 8 
billion in foreign exchange each year. The country has fossil energy reserves and a growing agriculture 
sector which has undergone a technological revolution during the nineties, registering a sustained growth of 
over 3.4 % annually. Because of its strategic political importance, Egypt receives a generous programme of 
international development assistance of the order of some U$ 1800 million per year 
In contrast to this, Egyptian social development indicators are unsatisfactory. A very modest human 
development index of 0.642 ranks Egypt 115 in the worldwide HDI classification, just above the list of 
countries with “low” human development index which commences at rank 127. Economic stability and 
accelerated growth has been accompanied by population growth (estimated at 2.1 per cent) and increased 
levels of poverty, particularly in some geographic areas. The very high levels of illiteracy undermine 
further improvements in human development. Population growth has given the Government cause for 
serious concern and ranks as one of the top national priorities. While Egypt has experienced a rapid decline 
in fertility since mid-80s, recent demographic projections indicate a slight reversal in this trend (at around 
3.5) over the past few years. With nearly 37 percent of the population below the age of 15 and due to enter 
childbearing years, the population will continue to grow, reaching 77 million by 2010 and over 120 million 
by 2030, and will require substantial investments in additional services (including basic education) and in 
reducing the incidence of poverty (particularly through employment opportunities, urban infrastructure and 
living facilities). With one million square kilometres Egypt’s entire population is concentrated in about 6 % of its territory, 
thus yielding an extraordinarily high effective population density (1300 persons/sq. km.) with consequent 
congestion and reduction in the quality of life. Particularly striking is the uneven distribution of population, 
namely the very high densities that are characteristic of the urban governorates. 
The difficulties posed by continuing population growth are multi-dimensional and relate to the increasing 
utilization of productive agriculture land to non-agricultural uses, the provision of adequate housing and 
shelter with basic amenities, and the quality of the environment. These issues continue to be overriding 
concerns of the Government, reflected by its long standing commitment to promote family planning, 
redistribute the population through creation of new settlements, and provide impetus for economic growth. 
Assuming that in the future mortality rates will continue to decline and net migration will not be significant, 
much will depend upon the future course of fertility, in particular in actions that will discourage early 
marriage, improve quality of health services and promote contraceptive use. Moreover, efforts to achieve 
economic growth and sustainable development will require an improved understanding of the linkages 
between population and development in context of the changing global and national environment and 
demographic dynamics, which may represent opportunities and challenges for Egypt. 
Egypt has obtained marked improvements in some important human development indicators such as school 
enrolment (96 %) infant mortality reduction (from 73 per thousand in 1995 to 55 per thousand in 2000) 
under five mortality reduction (from 96 per thousand in 1995 to 69 per thousand in 2000) life expectancy, 
access to safe water (96 % (urban) and 71 % (rural). While the trend is positive, the statistics conceal a 
persisting disparity that divides the Egyptian population along gender and income bracket lines and among 
rural/urban and lower/upper Egypt. An analysis of the effects of structural reforms on Egypt’s vulnerable 
groups (women, children, the indigent etc.) reveals the downside of the economic model and signals an area 
where the government could gainfully use a more coherent and systemic package of development 
assistance by the UN System. 
The baseline analysis on the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals shows overall positive 
progress in key areas of development, such as poverty reduction, curbing infant and maternal mortality, 
ensuring universal primary education, promoting gender empowerment and protecting the environment. 
However, the report reveals that progress has been higher in some areas (e.g. primary education and child 
mortality) than others (e.g. gender empowerment), and unevenly distributed in other cases (poverty 
reduction, reproductive health and the environment). The first MDGs confirms the need to sustain the 
efforts to put in place an efficient data collection and analysis system in order to improve the monitoring 
capacity of the institutions. 
2. Key Challenges
The rationale for a more concerted approach by the UN System to Egypt development problems stems from 
the need to ensure that, henceforth, Egypt’s successful structural and macro economic reform programme 
does not “exclude” a significant portion of the Egyptian population. What is called for is an adjustment of 
the government and the aid community development strategy so as to effectively re-orient those aspects of 
the economic development model and institutional practises that generate social exclusion and reproduce 
the phenomenon of social vulnerability and poverty. Egypt has the human, institutional, financial and 
technological resources and capacities to consolidate its market oriented development model while 
combating disparities that degrade the country’s human development index to levels which are 
incompatible with its standing as an international political leader. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt
14
The consequences of the events of 11 September 2001 on the Egyptian economy were significant. The 
Consultative Group (CG) meeting for Egypt that took place in February 2002 was able to take into account 
the effects of the war on terrorism on Egypt’s social and economic development. The CG meeting 
constituted a good opportunity to reaffirm the Government priorities as regards external assistance and to 
promote a policy dialogue with the international community on the most appropriate measures to be 
adopted in response to Egypt’s development challenges and to the new international context. 
To effectively address the problem of poverty and social exclusion the Egyptian government needs to focus 
on a wide range of multidisciplinary interconnected problems at the international, national, regional, 
communal and local level. It is therefore not a question of adding a social appendix to an economic reform 
programme, reshuffling budgetary allocations, adjusting a specific sectorial policy or fixing operational 
details in the delivery of a basic social service. It seems necessary to obtain a better understanding of 
critical social and economic development problems and their inter-relations, taking stock of national –
public and private- resources and capacities, drawing strategic and comprehensive action plans, coordinating external aid sources, and developing appropriate monitoring mechanisms for objective 
evaluation of progress made so as to obtain feedback for future policy formulation and program execution. 
In this respect, and taking its cue from the CCA diagnosis, the rationale for UN System intervention is to 
assist the government of Egypt in promoting a more people centred development strategy based on rational 
and efficient use of its institutional capabilities, natural resources and human assets. 
A: Institutional Capabilities
Egypt’s structural reform (ERSAP) was undeniably successful in reducing inflation, stabilising exchange 
rate and reducing fiscal deficit but macro economic policies still need adjustment particularly in regards to 
trade liberalisation, fiscal and custom reforms and the establishment of a legal framework more conducive 
to private sector development. The over 5 million staff strong government bureaucracy accounts for 25 % 
of the labour force and its ineffectiveness and behavioural patterns represents a formidable obstacle to the 
government’s reform and modernisation efforts. Over centralised government decision making undermines 
the effectiveness of public administration and its ability to provide practical solutions to local development 
problems. Concentration of administrative power and budget control at central level also discourages civil 
society, the private sector and NGO’s to contribute more effectively to a balanced and more equitable 
territorial development. The education system in Egypt is not fully adapted to the challenges of the time 
and fails to produce adequately prepared and skilled women and youth to enter the labour force. The 
National Health System is being gradually re-oriented towards a more holistic and personalised family 
physician type of medical care but this process needs additional impetus. Institutions concerned with 
preservation of natural resources have adequately trained technical staff but they lack the resources to be 
mobile and responsive and therefore fail to adequately address the problems at hand. Staff morale is low in 
the public administration. Egypt development is at a stage where it needs a more committed contribution 
from the private sector and civil society in general. To this effect the government needs to adjust fiscal, 
customs and labour laws so as to send a positive signal to the business community. The government also 
needs to take appropriate measures in order to re-orient social spending in favour of the disadvantaged 
groups and ensuring a more equitable income distribution. Insufficient use has been made of the capacity of 
the Non Governmental Organisation (NGO) sector to contribute to the country’s development. B : Natural Resources
Egypt’s natural resources include, first and foremost its cultural heritage that offers incomparable tourist 
attractions; water, both from the Nile and from groundwater desert reserves, fertile agricultural land 
alongside the Nile River, energy sources and the natural environment. Threats to Egypt’s natural resources 
come from inadequate protection of historical sites and agricultural land, urban encroachment on scarce 
fertile soils, wastage of water, soil degradation through poor irrigation practices, uncontrolled air pollution, 
scarcely regulated disposal of industrial emissions and effluents, and urban wastes. The CCA, the Donors 
Assistance Group (DAG) and the World Bank have addressed the issue of the effects of population density 
and concentration on the country’s natural resource base and the risks implied therein. The MDG baseline 
report has confirmed this concern and spelled out some of the main challenges faced by the country, such 
as for instance: understanding the interrelation between environmental issues and poverty, education, 
employment and health; further strengthening the institutions and their capacity to coordinate the 
formulation and implementation of environmental policies. 
C : Human Assets
A country’s greatest asset is its people. In Egypt, large segments of the population are not adequately 
attended to and do not have the opportunity to exercise their human rights on equal basis with the rest of the 
population. The government goals for improving the status of women, children, youth and urban and rural 
poor are laudable, however such groups remain neglected and cannot contribute their due to the country’s 
development efforts. 
Half the country’s population (women) enjoy little status or authority. About half of all Egyptian women 
are illiterate (this figure reaches 79% for female in agriculture and 86% of rural women headed 
households), many young girls in Egypt are deprived of educational attainments because preference is 
given to males; they are constrained by early marriage and child bearing; very few of them own assets; they 
are less present in the labour market than men and are concentrated in low productivity segments and lack 
adequate training opportunities; they are not well served in terms of access to health care, social security, 
sanitary and credit facilities. 60 % of working women in agriculture are unpaid family labour and do not 
receive any monetary compensation. Women in Egypt also have severe gender specific health problems. 
Over 50 % of women suffer from some form of reproductive tract ailment, almost all of them are still 
subject to genital mutilation between ages twelve and fourteen; 45 % of pregnant women have Iron 
deficiency anaemia and maternal mortality rates (measured at 174 per 100.000 births in 1993) though 
declining - are still high. There are also several issues related to women’s political rights and legal status 
which restrict their participation in public life and seriously curtail the contribution that women can make to 
Egypt’s development efforts in years to come. A large proportion of women is not even registered at birth; 
42% have no identity cards. Women have no permission to travel without their father or husband’s consent. 
Very few women are actively involved in politics in Parliament (3.3%) or in local councils (1.2%); there 
are no women judges in Egypt. 
Children and youth, which constitute 48 % of Egypt’s population, are another untapped human resource. 
Again, in the last decade the Egyptian government demonstrated political commitment and consistency in 
dealing with this problem and has obtained remarkable achievements in vaccination coverage, halving 
infant and under five mortality rates in less than a decade. Nevertheless, the 2000 demographic survey 
revealed that infant mortality rate is 41 per thousand live births and under-five mortality rate stands at 52 
per thousand. School attendance ratios, at 96 %, are high but up to 19 % of girls drop out of school in rural 
areas for several reasons including their low performance, the low valuation assigned to the education, UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

economic or family reasons. Average age at first marriage among girls is 19.5 years but it is estimated that 
14 % of women of reproductive age are married before the legal age of 16. Among married adolescent the 
average length of time between marriage and first pregnancy was 4 months. Two thirds of Egypt’s young 
people live in rural areas, where 64 % of the poor and 74 % of the critically poor live and have, therefore, 
higher exclusion risks. Children born in rural Upper Egypt still have records that clearly contrast with their 
urban or lower Egypt peers; 88 per 1000 under-five mortality rate and 41 per 1000 infant mortality rate (as 
compared to 52 and 41 national average). Illicit drug use represents a threat among Egyptian youth. There 
is increasing cannabis use, while raising abuse of heroin and pharmaceutical products has also been 
reported. Against the background of the youthful population structure of the country, there is a potential for 
exponential growth of this problem. The ultimate challenge youth poses to the country, according to the 
CCA, is that the Egyptian economy must create more than 650.000 new jobs every year to maintain a stable 
course, but the quality of preparation of youth for new employment opportunities is not aligned with the 
needs of a rapidly evolving and adapting marketplace. 
3. UN system experience in Egypt and lessons learned
The UN System has over 22 Agency and Programme Representatives in Cairo. The UN System direct 
programme delivery expenditures in Egypt amount to some U$ 50 million annually, not counting the World 
Bank and project co-financing from other sources (bilateral, IFI’s or the Egyptian Government). 
The UN system is heavily engaged in assisting the Government of Egypt in meeting its international 
obligations and in making its contribution to the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals 
(MDGs). UN agencies with a social agenda are managing programs to address pressing social development 
issues and upgrade Egypt’s human resources. UN programmes and the World Bank are active in a wide 
range of fields concerning the rational use and preservation of natural resources. The UN system is also 
most definitely making a contribution in the field of enhancing Egypt’s institutional capacities, including 
the modernization of its central and regional administration and the creation of a regulatory environment 
conducive to freeing up the economy so that it becomes more liberal, market oriented and internationally 
competitive. In the social side the UN is involved in assisting the government reform efforts in social 
sector institutions and in mainstreaming the rights of women, children and underprivileged groups with 
specific institutional policy objectives and budgetary allocations. The Annex on the status of UN 
Development cooperation provides a snapshot of UN sponsored programmes and projects in Egypt at the 
present time. 
Prior to drafting the United Nations Development Assistance Framework for Egypt the UN Country Team 
held several meetings to reflect on their collective experience with past assistance and on the lessons that 
could be drawn for future co-operation in this country. 
Agreement was reached on the need to pay particular attention to lessons learned in shaping the UNDAF 
strategy and identify priority areas for UN system intervention. The following basic lessons were very 
much taken into account: 
1. Experience has shown that the UN is most successful when it supports government in areas where it 
has comparative advantages and has established a best practise. 
2. It is of all evidence that while UN works through defined projects and country programmes , major 
impacts and radical improvements have been achieved in those areas where the UN and the 
government were able to maintain a deep and sustained policy dialogue for a prolonged period of time. 3. Given the relatively small amount of available funds, the UN in Egypt must concentrate its efforts: 
• At the policy advice level 
• In projects at the national or local level that result in practises which can be used for policy 
decision making (policy demonstration) 
4. Most benefits accrue when the UN is capable of assisting the government in establishing and 
maintaining close partnerships with other stakeholders. 
5. Achieving a noticeable improvement in cross cutting issues involving many disciplines and line 
Ministries will require a much stronger coordination effort than in the past. 
6. Reducing disparities in Egypt requires a more geographically focussed approach. 
7. Notwithstanding the above reducing disparities nation-wide among particular target groups (women, 
youth) will require a much improved use of already available resources and this in turn demands a 
more systematic approach in planning, targeting, implementing and monitoring of development 
activities. 
8. Increased involvement of the NGO sector is necessary in improving participation and maximising the 
effectiveness of services delivery particularly at the local level in impoverished communities. 
9. UN presence has often been instrumental in promoting policy reforms, building national capacities, 
influencing policy decisions and promoting the involvement of academic institutions, science and 
technology centres and private sector in the country’s development. 
10. Small, scattered, uncoordinated UN supported development projects have often not resulted in 
sustainable results. 
4. UN comparative advantages 
While its programme of assistance is substantial, the UN is clearly not a major donor from a financial 
perspective. Most UN offices have made a consistent effort to co-ordinate their programme of assistance to 
Egypt with those of major bilateral donors, the International Finaniel Institutions and, in some cases at 
least, with the NGO international community and their national counterparts. Some interesting development 
co-operation arrangements with the private sector and civil society organisations have also taken place. 
Though aid coordination has been and will continue to be a main concern of the UN, the system’s 
comparative advantages also call for UN development cooperation to reinforce its identity and bring its 
own contribution to bear on the country’s development efforts. In the particular case of Egypt the UN 
should make the best use of the following comparative advantages: 
• Recognised responsibility for leading the world community towards the attainment of the Millennium 
Development Goals. 
• Unique role as a neutral interlocutor of the government of Egypt, the donor community and Egyptian 
civil society. 
• Capacity to engage in a policy level dialogue on critical and crosscutting issues for Egypt’s 
development. 
• Collective field practical experience in combating poverty and promoting human development. 
During the period 2002-2006 the UN system in Egypt will continue to implement its programs and projects 
which contribute to build the country’s capacity to deal with development challenges, strengthen its 
institutions and represent a direct and tangible impact on the lives of millions of Egyptians either through 
direct assistance (e.g. immunisation, food aid, documentation) or indirectly (e.g. training educators, 
technology transfer, improved communications, enabling environments). Under the UNDAF the UN 
country team will join efforts and lend its collective assistance and political support to the Government of UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

In defining the goals for UN development assistance to Egypt in the period 2002-2006, due account was 
taken of the wide array of issues and problems in which the different UN agencies and programmes are 
involved at present and will continue to be involved in future by nature of their constitutional mandates. 
As stated before, the overarching goal of UN system involvement in Egypt is to promote more people 
centred development based on the rational and efficient use of the national institutional capabilities, natural 
resources and human assets. 
This overarching goal has been blended with the comparative advantages which the UN, as a collective 
body under one flag, can bring into the government’s development efforts during the period 2002-2006. 
With this in mind, three goals have been identified for the UNDAF that will both address the issues at hand 
and maximize the effectiveness of the UN system as a whole. Such goals are: 
GOAL I Enhanced governance through a more participatory policy dialogue, 
institutional capacity building and civil society empowerment 
Under this goal, the UN will assist all stakeholders in Egypt’s development to establish a common body of 
knowledge (facts, figures, trends, etc.) with regards to Egypt’s social and economic reality and a common 
understanding of the nature of development problems and constraints. This is a fundamental basis for 
deepening and widening a dialogue leading to well-founded recommendations for economic and social 
policy formulation and for legal and regulatory framework adjustments. The UN will, as a matter of 
priority, promote a dialogue on issues related to the attainment of MDGs consistently with the Government 
priority challenges. Policy dialogue will also be concerned with the country’s institutional preparedness for 
the challenges of the future. Increased stakeholder participation will improve governance, empower civil 
society and strengthen the administration capacity to deal with key development problems. UNDAF has 
singled out: an improved information base; a higher level participatory policy dialogue on key development 
issues; structural reforms with equity; provision of job opportunities; upgrading education and health 
strategies and the promotion of information and communications technologies as particular objectives to be 
addressed in the period 2002-2006. 
GOAL II Enhanced natural resources management, environmental sustainability and 
food security. 
Under this goal the UN system, including the World Bank, will lend its assistance to the Government of 
Egypt in achieving a more rational management of natural resources, and addressing the multiple threats to 
Egypt’s fragile ecosystem. Admittedly, many activities that fall under this goal require investments that are 
far beyond the possibilities of UN Funds and Programmes, but the UN system will still lend its 
international and country based knowledge and experience to guide, whenever necessary, the Government 
and its partners in their joint efforts towards this most critical goal for Egypt’s development during the 
period 2002-2006. As for Goal I, it will do so by promoting a common understanding of problems, and an 
open dialogue facilitating the involvement of civil society and NGOs, improving institutional coordination, 
sharing best practices and methodologies, institutional capacity building, information and training 
activities, and policy advice as required. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

Objective 1 – To Develop a reliable institutional data collection, analysis and Information System for 
People Centered Development.
Up to date historical records, census and survey data exist in Egypt and they are produced periodically by 
well established and professionally recognised institutions. The availability of data to users and to the 
public in general is not homogeneous and the quality and precision of estimates make it difficult to 
establish comparability over time and across regions. Different approaches or techniques for measuring the 
same phenomena have led to contradicting figures. Inconsistencies in basic data become particularly 
confusing when addressing poverty in Egypt. Disaggregation by gender, geographical location, age, income 
or ethnic groups is not always available. The CCA team, faced with varying estimates of key poverty 
indicators, set itself the task of harmonising statistical information and data analysis to get a clearer picture 
of the situation and prevailing trends. This exercise involved in depth discussions with government 
institutions, professional associations, international institutions and civil society organisations and revealed 
to what extent differences opinions could be reduced if data were presented in a clear and simple manner 
that permits greater focus and a common understanding. The CCA created its own data base of 
development indicators with particular emphasis on poverty and this was, made electronically available to 
all interested parties. 
 
A consistent and acknowledged data base needs to be complemented by a deeper understanding of the 
phenomenon of poverty which is not only lack of income but lack of human development in terms of 
health, nutrition, education and lack of opportunities for capabilities development. Several UN publications 
have thrown a new light on the nature of poverty in Egypt and flagged the critical strategic areas that need 
additional attention. It has also made a significant step forward in bringing consistency into poverty 
measurements in Egypt. The UN system will collaborate not only in producing a common and consistent 
flow of data and information on poverty but also by carrying out studies, submitting position papers and 
involving a wide range of development actors into the collection of data, analysis, discussion and 
understanding of the issues at hand. 
In particular the UN will support:

 Enrolment rates of children in primary school. 
 Gender disparities in primary and secondary education. 
 Infant and under five mortality rates. 
 Maternal mortality rates and births attended by qualified personnel. 
 Access to reproductive health services and contraceptive prevalence rates. 
 Environmental strategies for sustainable development with an emphasis on water. 
• Broaden policy research and evidence-based dialogue on population, poverty and development. 
• Preparation of a regionally disaggregated Human Development Report of Egypt.

• Promote an integrated, gender-sensitive information system on population for effective policy making

Objective 3 – To support government efforts in maintaining macro economic stability while promoting 
structural reforms, civil society empowerment, equitable growth and economic modernization
Reforms will be concerned with paving the road for Egypt to maintain high economic growth rate and 
stability. This will involve measures aimed at strengthening economic management, attracting foreign 
direct investments, fostering industrial modernisation, improving export performance, improve the quality 
and efficiency of the delivery of public services and promote employment opportunity and wage growth 
particularly in the more productive and competitive sectors of the economy. Egypt’s economic growth has 
come as a response to an increase in domestic demand not to the export sector. Cumbersome customs procedures and export finance restrictions have had a negative effect on exports. While increasing domestic 
consumption and raising standards of living of the Egyptian population should continue to be the driving 
force of the Egyptian economic model, external markets remain critical for ensuring a continued dynamic 
development of the private sector. 
Private sector development also needs a modernisation of the tax system aimed at increasing transparency 
and reducing discretionary incentives and distortions. The whole issue of government/private sector 
relations is undergoing a positive change and greater participation of the business community in national 
affairs is resulting. Civil service reform needs to show substantive progress and more participatory 
mechanisms involving citizens consultations in the preparation of development plans, the monitoring of the 
delivery of public services and granting of greater autonomy to local governments to find their own 
solutions to local problems. 
The UN, including the World Bank, in accordance with the respective mandates of its Agencies and 
Programs, will support: 
• Civil service reform. 
• Improved performance of public enterprises. 
• Reform of the Financial and Banking sector. 
• Decentralisation and local governance. 
• Industrial modernisation strategies. 
• Support new investment and maintenance strategies for the infrastructure sector. 
• The formulation and implementation of an Anti Poverty Action Plan. 
• Promote public/private partnership and dialogue concerning structural reform and privatisation. 
• Creating an enabling macro economic policy environment for the development of the private sector 
• Equity concerns in macro economic development (see objective 4 ). 
• Civil society empowerment. 
Objective 4 – To promote an economic and institutional environment conducive to the creation of 
productive job opportunities
Egypt had full low-productivity employment in the sixties, moderate unemployment in the seventies and 
eighties and a significant unemployment rise in the nineties in spite of a rapidly expanding economy. Job 
creation has clearly not been an automatic outcome of increased investment and economic activity, and the 
trend will not change direction in the absence of macro economic policies that include specific employment 
strategies. At present 68 % of individuals are employed by the private sector, 26 % by the government and 
the remainder holds jobs in public sector enterprises. With a staff of over 5 million the public sector cannot 
absorb additional personnel so, in the absence of migration to Gulf countries, it is Egypt’s private sector 
that will have to absorb the increasing labour force. Agriculture and manufacturing are the two labour 
intensive sectors in the Egyptian economy. It is estimated that the informal sector absorbs 40 % of the 
labour force whereas the modern sector is not labour intensive. Since 80 % of the women are not in the 
labour force, it is the educated young seeking first employment that swell the ranks of the unemployed in 
Egypt today. 
But the formal private sector will not blossom unless some general conditions are met and an enabling 
regulatory environment is put in place as stated above (see objective 3). An enabling environment for 
employment promotion should address, aside from the critical issues of shortage of invested capital and 
entrepreneurial skills, at least three additional outstanding problems. First government controls, licensing, 
taxes and labour laws are not conducive to the development of formal enterprises. Second, incentives need 
to be provided by the government for enterprises that invest in labour intensive sectors or technologies. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

Third, the labour force needs to adapt to the requirements of the expanding market for jobs and this requires

Objective 5 – To Upgrade Egypt’s health system
The overall health status of the Egyptian population shows remarkable progress over the last decades. 
Indicators of this improvement can be seen by the fall in infant and childhood mortality as well as maternal 
mortality. Life expectancy at birth for both sexes rose from 52.1 in the 1970s to 69.3 years in 2001. In 
recent years, tremendous efforts have been made to expand the network of health facilities. Currently, over 
95 per cent of the population have access to primary health care services. Despite this progress in the health 
status of the population, there is still room for improvement, particularly for certain population groups and 
in specific geographical locations (see objectives 10 and 12). Significant inefficiencies and inequities 
persist in the health system exemplified by the low hospital occupancy rates, excessive use of drugs, and 
surplus of physicians, and uneven distribution of resources. The progress as well as the main challenges 
related to child mortality and reproductive health has also been highlighted by the MDGs report. 
The health system still cover reproductive health needs under traditional vertical programmes for maternal 
child health and for family planning. Limited services are provided for other reproductive health 
components, such as for reproductive tract infections, cancer screening, sexually transmitted diseases and 
HIV/AIDS. Despite improvements in the coverage of antenatal care and medically assisted deliveries, 
further efforts are needed to improve coverage of services, particularly in the management of high-risk 
cases and provision of essential obstetric care. Postnatal coverage remains very low, particularly of home 
deliveries. As for family planning services, quality of care remains a major concern, as demonstrated by the 
high discontinuation rate (30 per cent of all users) of certain family planning methods. Furthermore, the 
reproductive health needs of adolescents for information and services are not adequately addressed and 
male involvement is very low. The MOHP is undertaking a process of health sector reform to enhance the quality, efficiency and 
sustainability of health services. The strategy is to adopt a comprehensive and integrated family health 
model for primary care representing a shift way from the vertical programmes, provide an affordable 
package of essential services delivered through both public and private health facilities, develop human 
resources to delivery primary health care utilizing the family health model, and to extend the existing health 
insurance system to finance this package of essential services. The family health model calls for greater 
participation of families and communities in health promotion and preventive care. The health sector 
reform has been piloted in three governorates, with the intention of introducing the reforms nation-wide 
based on the pilot experiences. 
Major health challenges facing Egypt include addressing the regional and socio-economic disparities, 
ensuring health care quality with sustainable financing, and promoting human resource development to 
increase the proficiency of health staff at all levels. Provision of comprehensive reproductive health care, 
particularly for adolescents, remains a priority. While the incidence of HIV/AIDS remains low, greater 
efforts are required to promote prevention and safe practices including possible impact in the work place. 
The UN system will support the Government in its efforts to meet these challenges through appropriate 
interventions both at the policy and operational levels. 
The UN system will support: 
• Adoption of the basic benefits package of services, covering preventive and curative health services 
• Adoption of comprehensive and integrated reproductive health services both at the policy and 
operational levels. 
• Promoting quality of care in service standards and practices (e.g. informed choice and appropriate 
counselling and follow-up), including in the provision of reproductive health services 
• Human resources development for all levels of health care, with emphasis on operationalizing the 
family health model and quality management. 
• Implementation of the revised epidemiological surveillance system. 
• Building an integrated health information system. 
• Operationalizing the national drug policy. 
• Fostering healthy lifestyles by enhancing positive dimensions of health, promoting environments, 
conditions and interventions supportive of healthy lifestyles and discouraging harmful attitudes and 
behaviour. 
• Supporting effective programmes for reducing mortality and morbidity, particularly among vulnerable 
groups and geographic locations. 
• Coordinating support for the national HIV/AIDS programme.

Objective 8 – Promote environmental protection
There are several serious threats to Egypt’s environment, both natural and man-made. Limited land 
resources are being lost through urban encroachment on agricultural land and inadequate irrigation 
practices which have already produced salinity problems in over 35 % of Egyptian crop lands. Wind 
erosion on desert border land is also a cause of soil degradation. Approximately 12 million tons of solid 
wastes are produced in Egypt every year and waste collection efficiency is 65 % in Cairo and less than 50 
% in the smaller cities. Putrefying wastes often find their way into drainage and irrigation canals with the 
consequent health risks for the population. Egypt has no facility for hazardous industrial or hospital wastes. 
Tourism influx and uncontrolled development is causing damage to fragile ecosystems such as Red Sea 
coral reefs, desert oasis or to Egypt’s cultural monuments. Air pollution is caused by desert dust and by 
environmentally uncontrolled industrial facilities, the burning of agricultural wastes and urban garbage, 
power generating stations and motor traffic. The air pollution’s values in Egypt major area centres are 
already above world recommended standards. Rapid urbanisation, specifically of the metropolitan areas 
(Cairo, Alexandria, Port Said and Suez), constraints the ability of urban settlements to offer a decent 
standard of living to citizens. Although precise figures are still lacking, the phenomenon of slum areas 
seems on the increase and requires an effective response. 
The Egyptian institutional and legal framework for combating environment problems is in place. The main 
problem is compliance and this in turn is a function of public awareness and attitudes. The government has 
strengthened its environmental institutions and created new environmental Agencies, an environment 
protection fund and installed a large number of monitoring stations throughput the country. The 
government has also taken public health protecting measures such as the introduction of lead free gasoline; 
moving industrial polluting plants away from populated centres; enforcing waste water disposal controls 
and making environmental feasibility a compulsory requirement for all new projects. Furthermore, Egypt is 
one of the very few countries in the world where the use of fuel cell as an alternative energy source to the 
combustion engine will be experimented thanks to UN support. 
UN assistance will target: 
• Compliance with International Environmental Law. 
• Support the implementation of the National Environmental Action Plan. 
• Greater involvement of the private and NGO sectors in environmental matters. 
• Promote greater inter ministerial and intersectorial co-ordination for ensuring uniform compliance with 
environmental laws and regulations. 
• Support environmental advocacy through public awareness campaigns.
• Continue its support for the development of cleaner energy sources. 
• Assist with the development and application of pollution control techniques in land, water and air. 
• Develop a deeper understanding of population dynamics and their impact on environment. 
Objective 9 – To ensure the population’s food security and nutrition
Egyptian population consumes predominantly wheat, maize, rice, potatoes, vegetables, fruits, milk, oil, 
meat fish and eggs. Domestic agricultural production does not supply all of the country’s food demand, but 
the deficit has traditionally been met through food imports. Imports of sufficient food have been possible in 
the past thanks to Egypt’s performance in securing foreign exchange. The government has traditionally UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

ensured food security to the population through its food subsidy program which started in the 1940’s and is 
regarded as emblematic of the government’s policy of social equity. The subsidy program covers bread, 
flour, cooking oil and sugar and has been instrumental in achieving relatively adequate nutrition levels in 
Egypt. Consequently the majority of the Egyptian population has a high caloric consumption and an 
adequate average daily intake of proteins (90 gm/day). Only 12 % of the population fall below the daily 
required level of 2100 calories per capita. The subsidy program faces some challenges. In the first place it 
represents a very high cost for the government (5 % of total budget expenditures); secondly it is not 
targeted to the needy and benefits all income groups. The CCA has flagged the problem of stunting (height 
for age) which still affects 1 in 5 children, and this goes up to 2 in 5 in rural Upper Egypt according to 
recent household surveys. The CCA also points to the need to get a better understanding of the dynamic of 
the household food economy and for advocating that food security becomes a priority issue in government 
development plans. 
The agricultural sector in Egypt pioneered the economic reform process on the eighties and introduced 
price and trading liberalisation measures that deregulated and privatised Egyptian agriculture to a 
significant degree. The dynamism of the agriculture sector has been a consequence of such policy reforms, 
of upgraded technological applications and of an expanded agricultural land base. Egypt agricultural 
development strategy is not based on maximising the growth of a particular sector or export crop but rather 
to waste the conditions for a more competitive production that can benefit from the Egypt’s accession to the 
World Trade Organisation and its new partnership arrangement with the European Union. 
UN assistance will target: 
• Support the government agricultural sector institutional reform programme to favour, inter alia, the 
participation of the private sector in agricultural research and extension services. 
• Strengthen the governments agricultural information system including production statistics, market 
opportunities and prices. 
• Support the expansion of the horticultural and livestock small holder sector with improved market 
information and services (post harvest, processing facilities, packing techniques, transport). 
• Promote trade policies to increase the competitiveness of Egypt’s agricultural export crops (e.g. cotton) 
• Develop adequate training programmes to re-cycle labour laid off by the re-structured state enterprises. 
• Enable self-reliant food security for the poorest by bringing agricultural and land settlement programs 
to the areas where the poor live.
• Adjust the food subsidies program and redirect food priorities to particularly vulnerable groups such as 
Bedouins, urban children at risk and school children in the poorest rural governorates.
Objective 10 – To maximise water use efficiency
The Nile river supplies 96 % of Egypt’s water. International agreements with other Nile countries limit 
Egypt’s use of new water to 55.5 billion cubic meters per year. Approximately 83 % of Egypt’s water is 
used in agriculture, 10 % in industry and the remaining 7 % by municipalities. Per capita consumption of 
water has fallen from 1,893 cubic meters per year in 1959 to about 900 in 1999. This figure is already 
below the recommended standard of 1000 cubic meters per person / per year. The CCA reports, that if no 
additional water resources are found and population growth maintains its present day momentum per capita 
consumption of water will fall to 670 cubic meters by 2017 and 536 by 2025. 
Water scarcity is not the only issue at stake. Water use and re-use efficiency, the development of water 
infrastructure works and water quality are all important strategic considerations for Egypt in the future. The 
government has many on-going programs and plans to tackle this problem. Rice and sugarcane varieties, 
the largest water customers, are being genetically selected on the basis of their low water requirements. Planting, irrigation and land levelling techniques that minimise water requirements maintaining yield levels 
have also been developed and put into practise. Re-use of agricultural drainage water is also being studied 
particularly with regards to its contamination from municipal and industrial waste water. The treatment of 
waste water for irrigation purposes is also being contemplated. 
Nile water which is the lifeline of Egypt receives polluting substances from agriculture residues, industrial 
and municipal wastes. The quality of Nile water deteriorates gradually as it approaches the Mediterranean. 
It also receives navigational effluents. This not only affects water quality, it also contaminates the soil and 
in some cases, crops and consequently the food chain. 
As regards access to safe drinking water, the MDGs report shows that Egypt is so far on track towards 
meeting the target of doubling, by 2015, the proportion of population with sustainable access to an 
improved water source. 
The UN system, including World Bank, will support Government’s and other donors’ efforts to: 
• Monitor water management throughout Egypt by achieving better co-ordination between urban and 
rural water agencies. 
• Institute a viable cost recovery and realistic water pricing system. 
• Create an enabling environment for the private sector to participate more fully in the. 
• development of the water sector. 
• Promote, wherever feasible, substitution of water intensive (rice, sugar) by water thrifty crops. 
• Continue research and development efforts to improve water quality and water recovery techniques. 
• Support the Nile River Basin Initiative.

Objective 11 - To promote a systemic and coherent action from all stakeholders to address the issue of 
gender disparity reduction in Egypt
Egypt subscribed to the Beijing Action Platform and ratified the Convention on the Elimination of All 
Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) in 1981 and although it explicitly maintained 
reservations in certain areas it has since enacted legislation to comply with the Convention and has 
undertaken plans and programs directly aimed at the elimination of gender disparities. Many important 
legal steps have been taken to improve the situation of women in the recent past and recognition must be 
given to many Egyptian nationals, in government as well as in the NGO and private sector, who are 
committed to realizing woman’s rights and equality before the law (e.g. on issues such as divorce, sexual 
violence, and the right to travel abroad). In 2000 the Egyptian government, with UN support, established 
the National Council for Women (NCW) which reports to the Office of the President and a clear mandate to 
mobilise government and civil society around policies and strategies for advancing the status of women in 
Egyptian society. 
In spite of the government’s laudable efforts, the situation in Egypt remains one of severe gender 
inequalities. Some of the objective data on the status of women’s education, health, access to goods, 
capabilities development opportunities and civil rights have been dealt with before (see p. 15). Some other 
issues are less objective or subject to change by law or decree. Although the rights of women to serve in the 
judiciary or in the legislative powers is conferred by law, very few women stand for election or are 
nominated by their parties because of perceptions that their candidatures will not be successful. The 
problem of female genital mutilation stems from the perception that a non-circumcised woman is not 
“clean” or apt for marriage and this notion is more rooted in tradition than in religion. Gender stereotypes UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

perseverance in school plays a major role in enhancing girls enrolment and discouraging drop outs; 
domestic violence and physical abuses are common and -according to recent surveys- they are at least 
partially justified by some sectors of the population including women themselves. Finally, recent studies

Objective 12: To promote a coherent and systemic action from all stakeholders to address the rights of 
Children and Youth
Children, adolescents and young people stand very high on the government’s priority list in recognition that 
this age group - up to 18 years old – represents 30 million individuals nearly 50 % of the Egyptian 
population and holds the key to the country’s development. The government has adapted measures to 
ensure that Egyptian youth today have much better chances of survival in the early years than in the past, 
grow healthy and obtain an enabling education to enter the labour force as productive adults. The 
government of Egypt has made formidable progress in these areas by adopting substantially sound and 
correct children and youth policies and programs. While the ratification of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child has been instrumental in shaping such policies and promoting new initiatives, their 
uneven degree of success is not due to a faulty technical approach but is rather explained by the lesser 
attention paid to young women and by the fact that two thirds of young people live in rural areas among the 
poorest strata of the population. In 1992 the Government has established the National Council for 
Childhood and Motherhood which reports to the office of the Prime Minister and will greatly facilitate 
addressing youth problems holistically in years to come. 
Concerning survival, almost the totality of Egyptian children -without gender discrimination- receive 
freely, through government health services, vaccination against all the vaccine preventable diseases 
(poliomyelitis, tetanus, diphtheria, tuberculosis, measles etc.). With only four cases of poliomyelitis 
registered in 2000 and two in 2001 (from 626 a decade ago) Egypt is well on its path to become a “polio 
free” country by 2005 as part of the world wide effort to eradicate polio. In the last decade Egypt has also 
managed to reduce infant and under five mortality rates by 60 %. This indicator reveals not only better 
health but also improved nutrition, housing conditions and a healthier environment, access to safe water 
and sanitation, Above all, it reflects an all important improvement of parental understanding of the basic 
requisites of child care including better handling of infectious respiratory and alimentary tract diseases 
which are the most frequent causes of preventable deaths in this age group. However, school age children 
still suffer from malnutrition problems, stunting and vitamin and mineral deficiencies. Again, these 
problems are much more serious in Egypt rural areas than elsewhere. Child labour in Egypt may concern up 
to 3 million individuals. Adolescent health problems are iron deficiency anaemia (50 % incidence) 
intestinal parasites (65 %) and stunting (18 %), while 86 % of female adolescent aged 13 to 19 have been 
circumcised. HIV / AIDS is not a major problem but awareness of sexually transmitted diseases is very 
limited thus signalling an area of risk for Egypt particularly in view of the HIV infection rate of its African 
neighbours. Teenage motherhood according to a recent survey was 9 % among persons aged 15 to 19, but it 
involved 20 % of the girls aged 19. This percentage was higher for less educated rural girls than for their 
urban educated counterparts. 
The law forbids marriage under the age of 16 for girls and 18 for boys, however among women of 
reproductive age, an estimated 14 % are married before the legal age of 16, exposing themselves to health 
risks associated with early pregnancy. Moreover, according to the Egypt DHS, married young women 
experience difficulties in accessing health services compared to older women. Various studies have shown 
that adolescents in Egypt lack information and knowledge of their reproductive systems and how to protect 
themselves. In the absence of parental guidance and education on reproductive health, young people seek 
information from less reliable sources and are vulnerable to risks. Neither children nor adults, adolescents 
fall through the cracks when it comes to reproductive health care. 
The greatest challenge for youth remains quality education and integration into the country’s labour force 
in a productive manner and to contribute to the economic expansion and modernisation of Egypt. At 
present, young people even the educated, are not particularly apt to participate effectively in a market 
oriented economy that requires international standards of competitiveness. 
The UN, taking note that the government of Egypt has made considerable progress in some areas, will 
provide support in the following: 
• Ensuring the sustainability of achievements in the field of immunisation, school enrolment and 
reduction in mortality rates by setting up reliable monitoring mechanisms. It will support national 
programmes in these fields and particularly in the eradication of polio, elimination of maternal 
neonatal tetanus, nutrition and prevention of HIV/AIDS. 
• Promoting and monitoring of the observance of children’s rights with particular emphasis on UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

disadvantaged youth and children at risk (street children, refugee children, child labour etc.), as well as

• Strengthen the capacity of coalitions of NGOs involved in monitoring the implementation of the CRC.
