Objective 13 –To promote a coherent and systemic action from all stakeholders to address the particular 
development problems of Rural Upper Egypt
Social indicators in the rural areas of Egypt governorates lag behind those of communities which are closer 
to the cities and urban centres where political and economic power is concentrated and where decisions are 
taken. The HDR for Egypt reveals that in at least 5 governorates (Assiut, Fayoum, Souhag, Qena and 
Menya) over 35 % of the population live in conditions of poverty. Infant mortality rates in Upper Egypt 
rural areas stand at 77.3 per thousand live births (national average 54.7); under five mortality at 98.5 per 
thousand (national average: 69); percentage of births attended by skilled personnel 38.2 % (national 
average: 61 %) percentage of pregnant women having medical check ups 19.2 % (national average: 36.7 
%); children suffering from malnutrition and stunting 25.8 % (national average: 18.7 %); total fertility rate 
4.2 % (national average: 3.5 %). Access to assets, land, credit, services, information and employment 
opportunities is also much lower in Upper Egypt governorates than in the rest of the country. Conventional 
government programs, often assisted by international co-operation, have been partially successful in the 
past but this is largely insufficient if the government has the ambition of seriously diminishing the poverty 
gap between Lower and Upper Egypt. 
Although the Government has been successful in reducing overall poverty levels over the past decade, the 
territorial distribution of progress is still very uneven, with projections for rural Upper Egypt suggesting 
stable or increasing poverty in the future. 
To definitely break the poverty cycle and revert the trend in these communities a much more coherent and 
systematic approach is called for. It is imperative to actively involve the affected population itself and assist 
them in getting organised to solve their own problems and to present a coherent demand of assistance needs 
for those problems they cannot solve themselves. It is equally important to strengthen local governments, 
both technically, managerially and financially and to give them a certain degree of autonomy and decision 
making power regarding the solution of local problems affecting the community. This implies first, a 
greater delegation of authority from central government on matters such as budgetary expenditure 
apportionment and decisions in their territory and second, local authorities’ capacity to influence the 
manner in which central basic services (education, health, sanitation, infrastructure) operate locally. 
In order to achieve this it is of fundamental importance to establish, through dialogue at the appropriate 
level), a closer connection between policy adoption at the national level (see objective 2) and field practices 
to combat poverty. This dialogue should be centred on poverty reduction strategies, decentralisation and institutional strengthening requirements, exchange of best practises for people’s participatory mechanisms 
and local services delivery; innovative anti-poverty methodological approaches, problem solving and 
suitable low cost technologies. International agencies must be part of this dialogue in order to obtain a 
clearer idea of where international co-operation practises must be adapted to increase their usefulness and 
impact. The dialogue should bring together the best poverty reduction practises at the local level, the central 
government policy decision making bodies at the central level and the international organisations that are 
engaged in the combat against poverty in Egypt. 
The UN will foster an understanding of the need for a holistic, multisectorial, participatory approach to deal 
with poverty problems and sustainable human development in Upper Egypt rural areas which will make 
full use in the UN system’s collective experience in Egypt in such fields as: 
• Strengthening local governance( empowering civil society, promotion of citizen consultations access 
to justice and community organisation). 
• Introducing participatory planning methodologies. 
• Local economic development (micro enterprises, cooperatives, credit, investment in infrastructure and 
services, technical and managerial support to business, harvesting and processing assistance, market 
opportunities and information etc.). 
• Community based facilities to promote universal access to sanitation and safe water, as well as 
hygiene promotion activities for school children and parents. 
• Decentralised health services and personalised care (targeting maternal mortality, micronutrient 
deficiencies, introducing the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) concept to health 
staff and supporting efforts to upgrade household management of sick child). 
• Primary and secondary community education services (ensuring no none is excluded from good 
quality basic education, promotion of community schools models with modern pedagogical 
approaches, parental education, psychosocial and cognitive development of children). 
• Food security. 
• Housing and environmental management. 
• Social protection services (protecting vulnerable groups, i.e. the elderly, single mothers, people with 
disabilities, working children). 
The UN will support the government in setting up criteria and suitable mechanisms for the selection of 
specific geographical areas or territories where this systematic approach to combat poverty could be put 
into practise. It will also assist the government in mobilising resources from the international community to 
support such integrated anti-poverty strategies. (see also Section V) UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

V. COOPERATION STRATEGIES
In making use of its relatively modest resources, the UN Specialised Agencies and Programmes in Egypt 
must privilege the unique qualitative value of their contribution as individual entities and as a collective 
force. The UN can help both the government, Egyptian civil society and the international community to 
tackle and eventually resolve some long standing problems that remain an obstacle to Egypt’s human 
development performance. The UN has in Egypt, as elsewhere, the advantage of its unquestioned 
international mandate on all matters related to the Millennium Development Goals, its political neutrality 
and tradition of respect for national sovereignty and its transparent administrative and financial procedures. 
The effectiveness of its aid, as judged inter alia by its high delivery rates, give it additional advantages for 
issues where joint multi-donor programming, pooling of resources or a co-ordinated approach is of the 
essence. In the particular case of Egypt, aside from global comparative advantages, the UN has 
accumulated credibility and prestige through its interventions in a variety of successful joint ventures with 
the Egyptian government. 
The UNDAF strategy stems from the conclusions of the Common Country Assessment. This document 
concludes that “Egypt has the knowledge and capacity to address the development challenges it faces. 
Putting the knowledge together in appropriate forms for policy makers, donors and the public and making 
certain that it is effectively shared for action is where the challenge lies”. The CCA concludes that the 
human, technical, institutional and financial resources to deal with broad development problems are 
available but poorly organised and co-ordinated so the end result falls below expectations. An effort is 
needed to pool these resources and organise activities in a more systemic manner so that people, 
technicians, the business community, NGOs, public institutions, funding agencies and national economic 
and political decision makers can act in greater harmony towards shared goals. 
1 Guiding Principles
The UN Agencies and Programs in Egypt will be guided by the following principles: 
• Full respect for the sovereignty of the GOE in setting its priorities for national development, in 
accordance with the country’s constitutional mandate. 
• Provide fullest and priority support to assist the GOE in meeting its commitments to the UN 
Conferences and the Millennium Development Goals. 
• Promote the observance of human rights including, social, economic, cultural and political rights in all 
its interventions including the elimination of any discrimination on the basis of sex, socio economic 
status, religion or race. 
• Support the strengthening of Egypt’s civil society and business community and encourage its increased 
involvement in national affairs. 
• Contribute to the development of national capabilities and ownership. 
• Promote the full participation of beneficiaries and their organisations in all field programs and targets. 
• Uphold environmental protection in every development intervention. 
• Promote the fullest co-operation between all UN Agencies and with other national and international 
development partners in Egypt both from government and non-governmental sector. 2 Advocacy
Most of the areas identified as goals of the UNDAF will require the adoption of policies laws and 
regulations by the executive and legislative powers of Egypt. They will also require a positive attitude 
towards change by decision makers, executive officers, politicians, opinion leaders and the Egyptian 
society as a whole. The UN will work to enlist the support of government and society leaders who can act 
as agents of change and produce a multiplier effect on the community at large. To do this, the UN must 
state its case clearly and present a solid front with a common opinion and a single voice. The UN Coordinator will speak for all issues that affect the entire UN System and will respect the leadership role of 
other UN Agencies in matters directly concerned with their respective mandates. In matters that affect one 
or more of the UN Agencies and Programmes the UN will strive to produce joint UN position papers. The 
UN will also promote, in agreement with the government, the holding of public fora to openly discuss 
different issues that may require changes. A major component of UN advocacy work has to do with public 
information and reaching the population at large. Publicity and awareness campaigns to bring about 
attitudinal readiness for the challenges of a changing world or for overcoming customs and traditions 
related to discrimination against particular groups or individuals will also be supported as part of the UN 
advocacy role under UNDAF. 
3 Policy Dialogue 
The Egyptian institutional and operational set up and the government’s administrative machinery have 
evolved through the years into an extremely complex system which, understandably, experiences difficulty 
in responding to social needs and economic stimuli in a timely manner. Many of the cross cutting issues 
that have been addressed by UNDAF touch on the duties and responsibilities of a wide variety of 
institutions which may not have a strong tradition of reaching operational decisions on matters of mutual 
interest by consensus. The heavy presence of international actors and the pressing need for further 
involvement of the private sector and civil society to adequately address some problems may not always 
facilitate matters in this respect. UN advocacy work, while necessary, may prove largely insufficient if no 
opportunity is provided to engage in a dialogue with those who have the authority and whose consensus 
and political commitment is necessary for changes to take place. As repeatedly stated in the rationale, goals 
and objectives of UNDAF, one of the key strategies for the UN system is to promote a more fluid policy 
dialogue in practically all the issues which have been identified as constraints on Egypt’s development. The 
size of the country, the magnitude and complexity of the issues involved, and their crosscutting nature, has 
in many cases rendered a frank participatory policy dialogue very difficult. The UN system in Egypt is 
convinced of the necessity to promote this exchange of views among all stakeholders on the development 
objectives identified under the UNDAF. Consequently, and taking full advantage of the UN’s recognised 
capacity to convene and assemble all concerned under its flag, the country team will strive, in full 
coordination with the government, to facilitate a wider policy dialogue on selected development issues. 
This upgraded policy dialogue with the government, and other national and international partners in 
development, constitutes one of the pillars of the UNDAF strategy. 
4 Aid co-ordination and partnerships 
The UNDAF strategy will fully utilise existing co-ordinating mechanisms with the government, the donor 
community and civil society to address key development problems holistically and in ways that can 
produce measurable and verifiable impact in the medium term. The most relevant co-ordination mechanism 
is the DAG–Donors Assistance Group, an informal network of donor countries that aims to improve the UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt

effectiveness of development assistance programmes. The UN Resident Coordinator acts as Chair to the 
Donor Assistance Group which is, in turn, composed of eight thematic sub-groups (1.Poverty / Social 
Development / SFD / micro-enterprise; 2. Gender and Development; 3.Participatory Development and 
Good Governance; 4. Health and Population; 5. Human Resources Development / Education; 6. Natural 
Renewable Resources; 7. Environment and Energy and 8. Private Sector Development). This Group is 
operating smoothly in Egypt and in good harmony with the Egyptian government counterparts which have 
fully appreciated the value of a donor co-ordination mechanism. The DAG is also valuable because it cooperates with the World Bank in harmonising donor positions for the Consultative Group Meetings on 
Egypt where the most relevant aid policy decisions and strategies to assist the government are agreed and 
pledges for continued development assistance are made. In this connection, and prior to the UNDAF 
exercise, the UN system actively participated in the preparation of a DAG Position Paper for the 
Consultative Group Meeting for Egypt. There are therefore excellent prospects for enhanced aid 
coordination in the period 2002-2006. 
5 Aligning Technical Assistance Programs
Most UN sponsored technical assistance programmes in Egypt are concerned with capacity building of 
government and non government institutions, promoting national ownership of development initiatives, 
particularly those concerned with more efficient delivery of basic services to the population, empowering 
organisations of civil society to assume a deeper involvement in the country’s affairs, feasibility and prefeasibility studies for investment projects or for budgetary resource allocations, natural resource surveying 
and monitoring, promoting the sustainability of development investments and safeguarding the 
environment for future generations. UN Agencies and Programmes an also engaged in a continuous policy 
dialogue with Government authorities at every level on matters of their particular concern. 
Further to the CCA exercise the Programmes of UN Agencies have been streamlined in at least two ways. 
First, the timing and duration of Agency programs has been set to coincide with the UNDAF time frame 
which means that henceforth the programming cycles of UN Agencies in Egypt will coincide. This is a 
valuable step forward because programme schedule incompatibilities has been a major obstacle to getting 
UN Agencies together at the time when the major programming decisions taken. Secondly, the programmes 
themselves reflect the findings of the CCA. This ensures a common perspective on the problems to be 
tackled and consequently opens the way for improved UN system co-ordination and program 
complementarities in the future. 
6 A coherent and systematic approach to deal with disparity reduction
The UN will strengthen the existing donor group co-ordinating mechanisms to address, in particular, 
objectives 11(gender) and 12 (youth) so that government political commitment, national resources, 
international funding and co-operation can be harnessed and re-oriented with a view to maximising impact. 
The UN, together with the government of Egypt and the DAG, will strive to establish a set of quantifiable 
targets to be met by Egypt, with external assistance by year 2006. In order to improve effectiveness, the UN 
will propose to all stakeholders to address specific thematic objectives related to women and youth in a 
more systematic manner. This approach can take many forms and be flexible in nature but it should attempt 
to include at least the following elements: 
1) Information base 
Reach a consensus on the present state of affairs with regard the particular issue (statistics, trends, bottlenecks, improved problem understanding). 
2) Targeting 
Set a realistic target to be reached by year 2006 in line with 2015 goals. 
3) Best practises Review 
A comprehensive review of best practises in Egypt, from government and other sources, that could be used 
for quick and effective mass replication in areas of need. 
4) Policy Working Group 
Utilize to the maximum extent possible existing policy working groups that can be used to reach consensus 
and adopt decisions related to the particular issue. Promote the establishment of a policy working group 
with relevant (multisectorial) government decision makers and civil society organisation representatives in 
cases such policy working groups do not exist. 
5) Action Programme 
Promote approval of regulations, policy reforms, national campaigns, action plans, programmes or projects 
as appropriate in accordance with the conclusions of the policy working groups. 
6) Resource Mobilisation 
Assist in resource mobilisation efforts at the national and international level to support the implementation 
as such plans and policies with a view to attaining targets as planned. 
7) Evaluation 
Establish joint monitoring and evaluation procedures on progress made. 
7 A Coherent and Systematic Approach to Rural Poverty Alleviation.
As per Objectives 10 and 11, improved donor coordination and civil society involvement will also be 
instrumental in assisting the government to increase the effectiveness of poverty eradication programs in 
Egypt’s most backward rural areas (Objective 12). The UN system can contribute by fostering a more 
coherent and participatory approach to combating poverty through the promotion of local development, 
including income generation and the provision of basic services. As for point 5.5, the specific approach can 
take many forms in accordance with local development plans, degree of autonomy, engagement of private 
sector and NGOs, number and relative importance of international cooperation partners, but it should 
preferably contain the following elements: 
1) Creating or strengthening a local development Working Group under local government authority (with 
the participation of private sector, civil society organizations, religious organizations, professional 
associations, NGOs, UN and donor community ). 
2) Designing in a participatory manner a comprehensive strategic plan to combat poverty. 
3) Reviewing best integrated development practices that could be applied in the area in question. 
4) Mobilizing resources for the implementation of an integrated multisectorial locally led venture. 
5) Strengthening local institutions to enable them to respond to locally expressed needs. 
6) Establishing a dialogue with government decision makers at the national and sectorial level on the need 
for policy reforms to promote local participatory development for poverty eradication. 
7) Designing policy measures and mobilizing government and donor community to permit the replication 
of successful practices in other economically depressed areas of Egypt. UN Development Assistance Framework – Egypt
